newsitem.title: UK: World generic drug sales to grow rapidly - IMS.
newsitem.headline: World generic drug sales to grow rapidly - IMS.

text.p: Sales of generic drugs in ten of the world's leading markets are set to continue to rise sharply in the next five years to around $22 billion, market researcher IMS International said on Thursday.
In a special report IMS said generic drug sales in the ten major markets totalled $13.8 billion last year, accounting for around ten percent of total drug sales.

"Growth is currently running at nearly double the retail market rate, driven by a mixture of government cost containment efforts and the patent expiry of major molecules in most countries and this looks likely to continue," IMS said.

Sales of generic drugs rose by a compound 11 percent a year between 1992 and 1996, with fastest growth in the U.S, up 16 percent, Germany, up six percent, Britain, up nine percent, and the Netherlands, up ten percent.

The report predicted compound growth in the ten major markets of ten percent a year between 1997 and 2001, with annual rises of 13 percent in the U.S, eleven percent in France and 13 percent in the Netherlands.

IMS said Britain, Germany, the Netherlands, Canada and the U.S. are leading the move to prescribing controls which encourage growth of generic drugs. Japan, France, Belgium, Italy and Spain are "late developers," said IMS, although all now had policies which promoted generic drug use.

It predicted continuing price wars between generic suppliers, although it noted that in the U.S. and Britain "where generic price wars have been damaging in the past, there are now tentative signs that the pricing situation is beginning to stabilise."
It said that for the "very popular blockbuster molecules" a large number of suppliers would lead to severe price competition.

The report cited the example of Bristol Myers Squibb Co's heart drug Capoten, which lost its U.S. patent in February 1996. Ten generic products containing the key ingredient of Capoten were launched following the expiry at a 90 percent discount to the price of the branded drug.
